title: The Sanodiya Brahmana of Mathura
html:
The Old Brahmana of Mathura

When Sri Chaitanya came to Mathura, the first to fall at His feet and dance with Him was an old brahmana of that city — a disciple of Sri Madhavendra Puri. He received the Lord in his home and fed Him, showed Him the holy places of Mathura, went with Him through the twelve forests of Vraja, and later, together with Balabhadra Bhattacharya, led Him away from Vraja and accompanied Him as far as Prayaga. Krishnadasa Kaviraja never once calls him by name: in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” he is “the brahmana,” “the Sanodiya brahmana,” “the disciple of Madhavendra Puri,” and of himself he says, “I am a brahmana of Mathura” (Madhya 17.179, 17.190, 18.129, 18.169). Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” calls him “the brahmana of Mathura, the disciple of Madhavendra,” and Narahari Chakravarti “the Sanodiya vipra” and “the best of the twice-born, dear to Gaura.” The biographies call him the Sanodiya Vipra, Sri Sanodiya Vipra, the brahmana of Mathura, the old brahmana, and, together with his Rajput companion, “the two Vrajavasis.” Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa call the brahmana who received the Lord in Mathura and guided Him through Vraja Krishnadasa; our database takes him to be the same person.1

Of his worldly life little is known. The biographies say plainly that we know neither his birthplace, nor his father and mother, nor even his name; the sources give neither the year and day of his appearance nor when and where he left this world, and his days are not found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. One of the biographies remarks that what matters in his life is not his origin, of which nothing is known, but the lessons of his example.

He lived in Mathura itself: so he says of himself before the Pathans, and so the Pathans address him — “You two are men of the west, from Mathura” (CC Madhya 18.169, 18.172). Murari Gupta writes, “There [in Mathura] a certain brahmana, best of the best”; Lochana Dasa, “There lived [there] a foremost brahmana named Krishnadasa.” When the Lord met him he was already advanced in years: “noble and simple-hearted, an aged brahmana,” the Lord calls him (Madhya 17.165), and the biographies call him simply “the old brahmana.”

By birth he was of the Sanodiya community: “that brahmana was a Sanodiya” (Madhya 17.179). One of the biographies adds that he was born into a family of brahmanas who served as priests to the “Sanovar” caste, that is, to dealers in gold. What this means, and why it matters for his story, we shall say below, when we come to the Lord's meal in his home.

One of the biographies calls him the Sanodiya brahmana “who kept himself hidden,” a resident of Sri Mathura. This is not secrecy but the concealment of a humble Vaishnava: he made no show either of his love for Krishna or of his discipleship under the great Madhavendra, and it came to light only when the Lord Himself came to Mathura.

Disciple of Madhavendra Puri

Long before the Lord came to Mathura, Sri Madhavendra Puri had come there during his pilgrimage. He visited this brahmana's house, gave him mantra, made him his disciple and ate from his hands. The brahmana himself would later tell the Lord:

“The brahmana said, ‘Sripada Madhavendra Puri came to the city of Mathura in the course of his wanderings. Out of kindness he came to my home. He made me his disciple and accepted his meal (bhiksa) from my hands. That great soul brought Gopala to light and served Him, and to this day Gopala is served at Govardhana.’” (CC Madhya 17.166–168)

By custom sannyasis did not accept food in the houses of Sanodiyas. But Madhavendra looked not at birth but at the heart:

“Nevertheless, seeing his Vaisnava conduct, Puri made him his disciple and accepted meals from him.” (CC Madhya 17.180)

One of the biographies puts it thus: Madhavendra saw in him a Vaishnava, that is, a pure brahmana, and therefore, against custom, made him his disciple and ate at his house. Another adds that by this Madhavendra showed how daiva-varnashrama works — the divine order in which a person is judged by his service to the Lord, not by his birth.

By his guru's mercy, says one of the biographies, love for Krishna awoke in him. It was this that the Lord saw in him when He asked, “Where did you get this treasure of love?” And he himself, seeing the Lord's love, recognized by it that the Lord was connected with Madhavendra: “Love for Krsna is found where there is a connection with him. Without him there is not even a scent of such love anywhere” (CC Madhya 17.173). One of the biographies cites these words in its chapter on Madhavendra and introduces them thus: wherever there is the prema of separation, there is surely a connection with Madhavendra Puri — and even the brahmana of Mathura “who kept himself hidden” recognized it in the Lord.

The Meeting at Keshava's Temple

This was on the journey when Mahaprabhu, after the Ratha-yatra, left Puri for Vrindavana, taking the forest way through Jharikhanda. Ramananda Raya and Svarupa Damodara gave Him Balabhadra Bhattacharya as His companion, and with him a brahmana servant. Through Kashi and Prayaga the Lord came to Mathura. The sources do not name the year of the journey; by our chronology the Lord's journey to Vrindavana and Prayaga falls in 1514–1516.

“Arriving in Mathura, He bathed at Visrama-tirtha, and at the birthplace He saw Kesava and bowed down to Him. Rapt in love, He danced, sang and roared again and again, and the people were astonished to see the Lord's rapture of love.” (CC Madhya 17.156–157)

And then our brahmana came to the Lord:

“A brahmana fell down and clasped the Lord's feet, and then, overwhelmed with love, he danced with the Lord. Dancing in love, the two embraced each other, and with arms raised they both called out, ‘Hari! Krsna!’” (CC Madhya 17.158–159)

The whole temple resounded with the name of Hari. Watching the Lord dance, the people said, “Love such as this is never of this world,” and concluded firmly that He was in every way an avatara of Krishna who had come to Mathura to deliver the people (Madhya 17.161–163).

Murari Gupta tells of this meeting in his own way. Seeing Hari, the brahmana lost all composure in love: his hair bristled, his voice faltered, and he fell at the feet of the Lord of the world. The Lord asked, “Who are you, good sir, whose composure love has shattered? By good fortune I have seen you.” And he replied:

“‘I am Your servant, O Lord, treasury of mercy. Though I am Krishnadasa in name only, yet I have had the good fortune of seeing You. O treasury of mercy, purify me with the dust of the Vaishnavas' feet, O Gaura, youthful son of Nanda!’” (Murari Gupta, “Sri Krishna-chaitanya-charitamrita” 4.2.10–11)

Krishnadasa means “servant of Krishna.” In Lochana Dasa, the Lord, at the very sight of Madhupura, cried “Akrura! Akrura!”, fell, and lay unconscious in separation for three days, while people came to look at this marvel. Krishnadasa, who lived there, saw Him and thought, “From where has this jewel among men come? Is this Shuka or Prahlada?” When the Lord asked, he told his name: “My name is Krishnadasa.”2

“You Are the Guru”

After the dance the Lord took the brahmana aside:

“Then Mahaprabhu took that brahmana aside, sat with him in private and asked him: ‘You are noble and simple-hearted, an aged brahmana. Where did you get this treasure of love?’” (CC Madhya 17.164–165)3

The brahmana told Him of Madhavendra Puri — how he had come to his house, taken him as a disciple and brought Gopala to light (Madhya 17.166–168). And then something happened that the brahmana had never expected:

“Hearing this, the Lord bowed down at the brahmana's feet, and the brahmana in fear fell at the Lord's feet. The Lord said, ‘You are in the position of a guru, and I am like your disciple. It is not proper for a guru to bow down to a disciple.’” (CC Madhya 17.169–170)4

The Lord, the Supreme Himself, needs no guru. But He keeps maryada — the proper order of relationships set for devotees — and honours this brahmana as the godbrother of His own guru, Ishvara Puri, a disciple of the same Madhavendra. So, in the words of one of the biographies, He teaches that the godbrothers of the guru are worthy of the disciple's reverence, and that all that is connected with the guru is to be honoured as the guru. And the brahmana falls at His feet in fear, for he knows Who stands before him.

He objected:

“Hearing this, the brahmana was astonished and said in fear, ‘You are a sannyasi — why do You speak like this? But seeing Your love, I infer that You have some connection with Madhavendra Puri; I am sure of it.’” (CC Madhya 17.171–172)

“Then the Bhattacarya told him of the connection, and hearing it the brahmana began to dance with joy.” (CC Madhya 17.174)

According to one of the biographies, the brahmana himself asked Balabhadra who the Lord's guru was and, his guess confirmed, rejoiced. Another says more: he realized that Mahaprabhu was the son of the king of Vraja Himself. The same sounds in Murari — “O Gaura, youthful son of Nanda!” — and in Lochana, where Krishnadasa tells the Lord, “I know for certain — You are the son of Nanda,” later, “Your sannyasa is only a disguise,” and at parting, “You are that very Krishna — this I have known for certain.”

The Meal in the Sanodiya's House

“Then the brahmana took the Lord to his own home and of his own accord rendered Him many kinds of service. He had the Bhattacarya cook for the Lord's meal, but Mahaprabhu smiled and said: ‘Puri Gosani has taken his meals in your house. You yourself give Me My meal — this is My instruction. “Whatever the best of men does, others do the same; whatever standard he sets, the world follows.”’” (CC Madhya 17.175–178)

One of the biographies calls the Lord here the guardian of daiva-varnashrama-dharma, which is favourable to pure bhakti: by the true meaning of the shastras He teaches the people. Another gives His words thus: “This I learned from his example.”5

To understand why the brahmana at first hesitated to cook himself, we must say something of his community.

“That brahmana was a Sanodiya, and sannyasis do not eat in a Sanodiya's house.” (CC Madhya 17.179)6

In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's edition the verse is headed: “because of his family by birth (shaukra), that brahmana's food is not accepted.” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya”: in the west the vaishyas are divided into Agarwals, Kalwars, Sanovars and other communities; the Agarwals are very pure, while the Kalwars, Sanovars and some others are held to have fallen through the faults of their occupations. The brahmanas who serve as priests to the Kalwars and Sanovars are called Sanodiya brahmanas; the Sanovars are dealers in gold, and their priests are the “Sanovar brahmanas.” Because they serve as priests to such communities, they themselves are counted as fallen, and sannyasis do not eat in their houses. The biographies give this explanation almost word for word.7

This reasoning concerns the social standing of a family by birth, not a judgment of the brahmana himself. He is a Vaishnava, a disciple of Madhavendra, and one of the biographies calls him outright “a pure brahmana.” And Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, speaking of how Sri Chaitanya regarded caste distinctions, writes that the Lord never saw caste in His devotees: He did not take food from non-devotees who merely called themselves brahmanas, but from Vaishnava brahmanas, from brahmanas who chanted a lakh of Hari's names, and even from the hand of a Sanodiya, from whom by custom not even water was accepted, He accepted food, seeing their devotion to Hari and regarding them as brahmanas whose food may be eaten (“Sri Chaitanya-darshane,” p. 635).

The brahmana answered the Lord humbly:

“‘To give You a meal is my great good fortune. You are the Lord; You are not bound by rules of conduct. But foolish people will censure You, and I will not be able to bear the words of those wicked people.’” (CC Madhya 17.182–183)

He spoke the truth: the Lord is bound by no rules. And he feared not for himself but for the Lord's good name: by the custom of the time fools would revile a sannyasi who had eaten in a Sanodiya's house. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya” why the brahmana speaks so. This pure devotee did not by birth belong to those from whose hands water is accepted, yet he was established in the truth and in daiva-varnashrama, which is favourable to bhakti — and therefore, without fear or hesitation, he called “fools” and “wicked” the followers of adaiva-varnashrama, the worldly caste order: those who oppose Mahaprabhu and pure bhakti, see caste in a Vaishnava and quarrel about maha-prasada.

And yet the Lord, free from all rules, follows for the people's instruction the conduct of the great devotees. He replied:

“The Lord said, ‘The sruti, the smrti and all the sages are not of one opinion; they teach many different kinds of dharma. The conduct of a sadhu is what establishes dharma, and the conduct of Puri Gosani is the essence of dharma.’” (CC Madhya 17.184–185)

And He cited the verse of the “Mahabharata”: the path is the one by which the mahajanas, the great souls, have gone (Madhya 17.186).

Thus Madhavendra, and after him the Lord Himself, by accepting food from a Sanodiya, showed what daiva-varnashrama is: a Vaishnava is judged not by social rank, and dharma is set by the conduct of the mahajanas, not by custom.

“Then the brahmana served the Lord His meal.” (CC Madhya 17.187)

Govinda-deva tells the same briefly:

“Seeing Him as a wonder, a certain brahmin of Mathura, a disciple of Madhavendra in that forest land, joyfully, honouring [Him] as a guru, brought the Lord to his home and fed Him.” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.14)

And the Lord, he goes on, was pleased with his devotion (14.15). In Murari, having gone round Mathura, the Lord gladly accepted bhiksha in Krishnadasa's house, and afterwards, while Krishnadasa served His feet, spoke of the sweetness of Krishna's bliss (4.4.24–25). In Lochana the Lord spent that day in Krishnadasa's house, and all night Krishnadasa told Him of the Mathura-mandala.

After the meal all Mathura came to the brahmana's house: “people came by the hundreds of thousands, beyond counting.” The Lord came out to them, raised His arms and called out, “Haribol!” — and the people danced, mad with love, calling out the name of Hari (CC Madhya 17.187–189).

Guide Through Mathura and Vraja

From that day the brahmana became the Lord's guide.

“The Lord bathed at the twenty-four ghats of the Yamuna, and the brahmana showed Him the holy places. He saw Svayambhu, Visrama, Dirgha-visnu, Bhutesvara, Mahavidya, Gokarna and many other places.” (CC Madhya 17.190–191)

Govinda-deva too writes that the Lord saw the many holy places of Mathura “with that brahmin of Mathura” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.16).

“When the Lord wished to see the forests, He took that same brahmana with Him.” (CC Madhya 17.192)

So he became the Lord's companion in going round the twelve forests of Vraja; one of the biographies recalls how with him the Lord went round the forests, listening to the parrots' talk. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura lists these forests: east of the Yamuna — Bhadra, Bilva, Loha, Bhandira and Maha; west of it — Madhu, Tala, Kumuda, Bahula, Kamya, Khadira and Vrindavana itself. One of the biographies, too, draws on Madhya 17.164–168 and 17.192 when it speaks of him in its chapter on Madhavendra.

Once in the forest the Lord saw the necks of peacocks, whose hue called Krishna to His mind, and fell unconscious. The brahmana was at hand:

“Seeing the Lord unconscious, the brahmana and the Bhattacarya tried to revive Him. Hurriedly they took Mahaprabhu's outer cloth, sprinkled His body with water and fanned Him with the cloth. They spoke the name of Krsna loudly in the Lord's ear.” (CC Madhya 17.219–221)

Coming to Himself, the Lord sprang up crying “Say it! Say it!” and went on, dancing.

“The Bhattacarya and the brahmana sang the name of Krsna, and the Lord went on along the path, dancing all the way. The brahmana was amazed to see the Lord's rapture of love, and he grew anxious about how to keep the Lord safe.” (CC Madhya 17.224–225)

The Lord's unconsciousness is not the swoon of a sick man but the depth of His love for Krishna, and the brahmana's service was care for the Lord immersed in prema.

He was with the Lord further on as well. At Arishtagrama the Lord asked where Radha-kunda was, but neither the local people nor “the brahmana with Him” knew — and the all-knowing Lord Himself revealed the forgotten holy place (CC Madhya 18.4–5). Returning from Gokula to Mathura, the Lord “stayed in the house of that same brahmana” — at the house of Madhavendra Puri's disciple, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains — and then, because of the crowds, went away to secluded Akrura-tirtha (Madhya 18.69–70). From there, according to Govinda-deva, He went again in the morning to Vrindavana “with those two brahmins” — that is, with him and with Balabhadra (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.43).

While the Lord stayed at Akrura-tirtha, the brahmana served Him in his own way:

“That brahmana, the disciple of Madhava Puri, arranged invitations for the Lord in house after house in Mathura.” (CC Madhya 18.129)

Ten or twenty invitations came each day; Balabhadra accepted only one, and those who could not invite the Lord themselves pleaded with the Sanodiya brahmana to persuade Him (Madhya 18.130–132). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his heading to these verses, says: the Sanodiya brahmana gives all the pious people of Mathura the chance to serve the Lord and so delivers them.

Krishnadasa in Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa

Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa tell of the Lord's guide in Vraja at much greater length than Kaviraja Gosvami. In Murari, hearing his answer, the Lord says: “It is you who are truly a servant of Krishna. For you know all the secret pastimes of Sri Krishna's abode — tell them, O best of men!” Krishnadasa asks, “Place Your feet in my heart and reveal Your own Madhu-mandala,” and the Lord answers in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:

“‘By My command may the pastimes of Sri Krishna and the holy places shine forth to you with ease on every side.’” (Murari Gupta 4.2.14)

Krishnadasa promised to show Him everything, danced and wept, and that night they talked of the pastimes of Vraja.

In Lochana the Lord asks to be shown the Mathura-mandala “place by place.” The brahmana answers, “I do not know all the places; I know only the places of the twelve forests.” The Lord laughs in the bliss of prema and manifests His power in his body — and he says, “I will show everything; from Krishna's birth to the slaying of Kamsa — I will tell it all.” The Lord embraces him.

Here it matters to understand what is taking place. The Lord “asks” about the holy places and “asks to be shown” them — but this is the play of One who is Krishna Himself; not for nothing does Lochana say, “Ishvara Himself plays a prank on Krishnadasa.” And that the Lord “manifested His power in his body” is the bestowal of power, shakti-sanchara, by which a Vaishnava reveals what is hidden: not worldly inspiration nor a guide's know-how, but the Lord's mercy disclosing His own pastimes.

Further on, in both poets, Krishnadasa describes to the Lord the Yamuna and the twelve forests — seven on the western bank and five on the eastern; shows Him Mathura — its walls, Kamsa's palace, the prison, the houses of Uddhava and Kubja, the arena, Gatashrama, the ghats; tells Him of the measure of the Mathura-mandala — eighty-four kroshas — and of the lake Setubandha; ferries the Lord across the Yamuna to Mahavana and leads Him through Vrindavana, Govardhana, Nandishvara, and the Khadira, Kumuda and Ambika forests, telling of Akrura and of the slaying of Kamsa. In Murari, at the Lord's thunderous “hum” “the best of brahmanas was frightened” and, joining his palms, went on with his account; on a sleepless night the Lord begs him, “Krishnadasa, speak to Me! This night torments Me”; and hearing of the divine Child, the Lord embraces him with love. In Lochana, seeing a grove of ashokas burst into bloom at the Lord's glance, Krishnadasa says, “Your sannyasa is only a disguise,” and weeps at His feet. These accounts themselves are about Krishna's pastimes, not about him, and we do not retell them here.

In both poets the parting takes place in Vraja. In Murari, when Krishnadasa had shown the Lord the whole Vraja-mandala, the Lord said:

“‘As the nectar of the rasa of Krishna's stories has softened My heart, so may Krishnachandra Himself be gracious to you.’ He replied, ‘I am Your servant, and You are Krishna, the abode of Shri. Make it so, O Lord, that I know no one but You.’” (Murari Gupta 4.13.2–3)

The Lord blessed him, embraced him and departed “surrounded by brahmanas.” In Lochana Krishnadasa, falling at His feet, entreats Him: “I am in great distress — do not go away, deceiving me! You are that very Krishna — this I have known for certain,” and the Lord answers: “By your grace I have seen the secret places… may Krishna be gracious to you, Krishnadasa!” According to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita,” however, the Sanodiya brahmana did not part from the Lord in Vraja but went on with Him as far as Prayaga.8

Leading the Lord Away from Vraja

In Vraja the Lord's love grew day by day. Once, sitting on the bank at Akrura-tirtha, He remembered that here Akrura had seen Vaikuntha and the people of Vraja Goloka, sprang up and threw Himself into the water. Krishnadasa the Rajput cried out, and Balabhadra leapt in after Him and pulled Him out (CC Madhya 18.135–138). Then Balabhadra turned to our brahmana:

“Then the Bhattacarya took that brahmana aside, and sitting in a secluded place they made a plan. ‘Today I was here, and I pulled the Lord out. But if He dives in at Vrndavana, who will pull Him out? The crowds of people, the bother of invitations, the Lord's constant absorption — none of this seems good to me. If we take the Lord away from Vrndavana, all will be well. This is a good plan.’” (CC Madhya 18.139–142)

The biographies say the same: Balabhadra, alarmed by the Lord's frequent transformations of love, consulted “Sri Sanodiya brahmana, the disciple of Madhavendra Puripada,” and they decided that the Lord must not be left wandering in Vraja. Govinda-deva writes that Balabhadra consulted “in private with the brahmin of Mathura,” alarmed by the invasion of the crowds (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.53).9

How to lead the Lord away was the Sanodiya brahmana's own idea:

“The brahmana said, ‘Let us take the Lord to Prayaga. If we go by the road along the bank of the Ganga, the journey will be pleasant. Let us first go to Soro-ksetra and bathe in the Ganga, and then travel on that road with the Lord. The month of Magha has begun. If we go now, we shall have some days of bathing at Prayaga during Makara. Tell Him something of your own distress, and mention the full moon of Makara (makara-pancasi) at Prayaga.’” (CC Madhya 18.143–146)10

Balabhadra told the Lord both of his distress and of this plan. The Lord had no wish to leave Vrindavana, but to fulfil His devotee's wish He answered, “You brought Me here and showed Me Vrndavana. I shall never be able to repay this debt. Whatever you wish, that I will do” (CC Madhya 18.152–154). The biographies add that the Lord accepted the counsel also out of reverence for the Sanodiya brahmana as the godbrother of His guru; one of them says the Lord could not refuse him. The one does not exclude the other.11

The brahmana knew the road along the Ganga:

“Krsnadasa, full of love, and that brahmana — these two knew the road along the Ganga well.” (CC Madhya 18.158)

So he and Krishnadasa the Rajput went along as guides. Govinda-deva writes that the Lord departed with five companions — three followers from Gauda and two devotees from Mathura — and that the eminent people of Mathura, stricken with grief, followed Him (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.57).12

Before the Pathans

On the way, seeing that His companions were tired, the Lord sat down beneath a tree. Cows were grazing nearby; the Lord felt the pastimes of Vraja, and when a cowherd boy played on his flute He fell unconscious, without breath, foam on His lips. This was the swoon of love. But ten Pathan horsemen led by Bijli Khan thought otherwise: these four had drugged the sannyasi, killed Him and robbed Him (CC Madhya 18.159–165).

“Then the Pathans bound the four men and wanted to cut them down. The Bengalis all began to tremble. Krsnadasa was a Rajput and utterly fearless. That brahmana too was fearless, and very bold of speech.” (CC Madhya 18.166–167)

The Bengalis — Balabhadra and his companion — trembled, while the two local men — the Rajput and the brahmana of Mathura — were not afraid and found what to say.

“The brahmana said, ‘Pathan, I appeal to you in the name of your padsah! Come along — I will go with you before the sikdar. This sannyasi is my guru, and I am a brahmana of Mathura. I have a hundred men at the padsah's court. Because of an illness this sannyasi sometimes faints. He will soon regain consciousness and come to His senses. Sit here a moment and keep us all bound. Ask Him, and then kill me.’” (CC Madhya 18.168–171)13

“Illness” — so the brahmana speaks to strangers, to save his companions and not to reveal to them what is hidden; the Lord's unconsciousness at the sound of the flute is a manifestation of mahabhava, the highest love, not a disease. And the leader judged:

“The Pathan said, ‘You two are men of the west, from Mathura, and these two Bengali cheats are trembling.’” (CC Madhya 18.172)

Then Krishnadasa the Rajput threatened the Pathans, and at that moment the Lord came to Himself and, loudly calling “Hari! Hari!”, began to dance. The Pathans in fear released the four, and the Lord never saw His companions bound. He said to the Pathans:

“‘They are not cheats; they are My companions. I am a mendicant sannyasi and have no wealth at all. Because of the falling sickness I sometimes lose consciousness, and these four kindly look after Me.’” (CC Madhya 18.183–184)

“The falling sickness” — in the Bengali mrigi — is the same veil the brahmana had used before: so before strangers the Lord conceals His prema. Our brahmana is one of the “four” whom the Lord called His companions. He was present, too, when the Lord refuted the arguments of the pir and converted Bijli Khan and his men (Madhya 18.185–212); of this we tell in the account of Bijli Khan.

As Far as Prayaga

“At Soro-ksetra the Lord bathed in the Ganga, and then He set out for Prayaga by the road along its bank. There the Lord bade farewell to that brahmana and to Krsnadasa, but the two folded their hands and said: ‘We two will go with You as far as Prayaga. Where shall we ever again find the company of Your feet? This is a land of mlecchas, and someone somewhere may make trouble. The Bhattacarya is a scholar; he does not know how to talk to them.’” (CC Madhya 18.214–217)

According to one of the biographies, the Lord, in sending them back, said: “You have taken great pains to come from Mathura and show us the road; I would not burden you any longer — return from here.”

“Hearing this, Mahaprabhu smiled slightly, and the two went on with the Lord.” (CC Madhya 18.218)

In their plea the first thing is the wish to be with the Lord a little longer — “Where shall we ever again find the company of Your feet?” — and only then their concern: this is a land of mlecchas, trouble may arise on the way, and Balabhadra would not manage with strangers.14

Reaching Prayaga, the Lord bathed for ten days at the confluence of the Ganga and the Yamuna in the days of Makara (CC Madhya 18.222). Of the brahmana himself the sources are then silent: neither the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” nor the biographies tell of his return to Mathura or of when he left this world.

His Memory

Years later, when Raghava Pandita was guiding Srinivasa and Narottama through Mathura, he first brought them to the place where the Sanodiya vipra had lived. Narahari Chakravarti writes in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” that this was the one in whose house Sri Krishna Chaitanya accepted bhiksha — the disciple of Madhavendra Puri Gosvami, who had seen the highest secret of Gauranga. “Here Gaurachandra danced, rapt in love; countless people came, all went mad in the kirtana of the name… all knew Him to be the son of the king of Vraja,” Raghava told them; and Srinivasa and Narottama, listening, wept and rolled in the dust of the brahmana's courtyard (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 5.163–171).

Further on, as he guided them through Vraja, Raghava recalled him twice more. At Raval he told Srinivasa that Gaurachandra with His companions, coming from Gokula, had stayed there, while people came running, called out “Hari!” and said, “This is surely Krishna — in this form He wanders through Vraja as He pleases”; and, “having shown here a pastime beyond this world, the Lord went to Mathura with that Sanodiya” (5.1828–1835). And at Imli-tala Raghava told how the Lord, under the cover of a sannyasi, came into the Mathura-mandala and, taking the Sanodiya vipra of Mathura with Him, wandered through Vraja in the rapture of bhakti with great joy: about the pastimes He Himself had once performed He asked everyone as though He did not know — so sweet it was to Him to hear of them from others' lips (5.2225–2228). This is the same play of which Murari and Lochana speak: Krishna Himself “asks” about His own pastimes for the sweetness of hearing of them from His devotees.

In the “Namamrita-samudra” the same Narahari Chakravarti, among the prayers in which he asks the Lord's associates for Vaishnava virtues and for faithfulness to the holy land, turns to him as well — with a prayer for Mathura:

“O best of the twice-born, disciple of Madhavendra, dear to Gaura! Grant [me] unceasing residence in the Mathura-mandala.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 215)

One of the biographies further writes that later Sanatana Gosvami went round the twelve forests of Vraja together with Subuddhi and the Sanoriya brahmana, and learned from them that Rupa and Anupama had shortly before made the same round and left by the road along the Ganga.15

Significance

Of the Sanodiya brahmana we know almost nothing beyond the days he spent with the Lord; yet much was contained in those days. His discipleship under Madhavendra and the Lord's meal in his house showed what daiva-varnashrama is: a Vaishnava is judged by his devotion, not by his birth, and dharma is set by the conduct of the mahajanas. The Lord's bow to him taught that all that is connected with the guru — the guru's godbrothers too — is to be honoured. And he himself, recognizing the Lord's connection with Madhavendra by His love alone, showed that the prema of separation knows its own source. He kept himself hidden, as befits a humble Vaishnava, and all that is known of him is his service: he danced with the Lord, fed Him, guided Him to the holy places, watched over Him in the swoons of love, fearlessly stood up for his companions before the Pathans, and would not part from the Lord while he could still walk at His side.

Notes

  1. Neither Krishnadasa Kaviraja nor the biographies give his name; one of the biographies says plainly that not even his name has come down to us. The name “Krishnadasa” appears only in Murari Gupta (4.2.11) and Lochana Dasa (Shesha-khanda, “The Lord Sees Vrindavana,” 48, 52). It is our database that takes him to be the same person as the Sanodiya brahmana of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita”: both have the same role — he received the Lord in Mathura, fed Him and guided Him through Vraja. But there are differences: Murari and Lochana do not say that he was Madhavendra's disciple, and in them he parts from the Lord in Vraja, whereas in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” the Sanodiya brahmana went with Him through Soro-kshetra as far as Prayaga. We tell the story according to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita.” He is not to be confused with Krishnadasa the Rajput, his companion on the way from Vraja to Prayaga, nor with Kala Krishnadasa, Krishnadasa of Badagachhi, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, or Krishnadasa the disciple of Vallabhacharya, the manager of Gopala's temple at Govardhana.
